hooks.text: A massive asteroid once reached the highest hazard rating in history.
Will a skyscraper-sized asteroid actually collide with Earth in 2029?
A terrifying doomsday asteroid is not actually going to hit Earth.

title: The Day an Asteroid Will Pass Closer Than Our Satellites
description: In 2029, the notorious asteroid Apophis will make an unprecedented flyby, passing closer to Earth than our own geostationary satellites.

beats.text: A massive asteroid once reached the highest hazard rating in history.
beats.visual: illustration of asteroid Apophis approaching a glowing Earth, NASA, 2020

beats.text: Discovered in 2004, asteroid Apophis was given a 2.7 percent chance of slamming into Earth.
beats.visual: photograph of the Kitt Peak National Observatory telescope domes at dusk, 2004

beats.text: But radar observations in March 2021 definitively ruled out any collision for at least a century.
beats.visual: photograph of the Goldstone Deep Space Communications Complex antenna in California, 2021

beats.text: Yet, on Friday, April 13, 2029, the 450-meter rock will still make history.
beats.visual: radar delay Doppler image of asteroid Apophis, Goldstone Observatory, 2021

beats.text: It will sweep less than 32,000 kilometers above us, passing closer than our geostationary satellites.
beats.visual: diagram showing geostationary satellite orbits and the flyby path of Apophis, ESA, 2024

beats.text: Billions of people in Europe, Africa, and Asia can watch it with the naked eye.
beats.visual: illustration of asteroid Apophis as a point of light in the night sky, ESA, 2024

beats.text: During this flyby, Earth's gravitational tidal forces will twist the asteroid and trigger surface movements.
beats.visual: artist concept of tidal forces stretching the surface of asteroid Apophis, ESA, 2024

beats.text: This intense cosmic encounter will forever alter the orbit of the massive asteroid.
beats.visual: diagram of asteroid orbit changing from Aten to Apollo class, NASA, 2024

better_than_last: We improved the hook by creating a strong curiosity-gap statement that seamlessly loops with the final line of the video.
